keyQuestions.question: How aggressively will Takeda defend Takhzyro share against oral entrants?
keyQuestions.answer: Aggressively but indirectly. The strategy pattern (RWE generation, patient services, label expansion) shows defense through stickiness rather than direct clinical confrontation. Expect amplified patient-experience messaging through 2026 to 2027.

keyQuestions.answer: Strongest in US, Germany, Japan. Moderate in France and UK. Weaker presence in Italy and Spain creates potential access windows for oral on-demand early adoption.

name: BioCryst
oneLineDescription: First-to-market oral HAE therapy with Orladeyo (prophylaxis); smaller commercial footprint, HAE-focused organization.
executiveSummary: BioCryst validated the oral modality in HAE with Orladeyo's 2020 approval and has built a commercially meaningful prophylaxis franchise. Growth has moderated as the early adopter pool is converted. The company is pursuing pediatric expansion and formulation lifecycle work but has no oral on-demand program, positioning BioCryst as a modality ally and a patient-share competitor rather than a direct threat to sebetralstat.

keyQuestions.question: Will BioCryst pursue an oral on-demand program?
keyQuestions.answer: No visible program. Pipeline investment has concentrated on extended-release prophylaxis and pediatric label expansion. BioCryst is structurally a prophylaxis company; entering on-demand would require a mechanism shift, which has not been signalled.

keyQuestions.question: Is BioCryst a partner, a competitor, or both?
keyQuestions.answer: Both, but weighted toward competitive. They validate the oral modality thesis publicly (helpful for sebetralstat) but compete for the same patient budgets and physician mindshare. Treat them as modality allies in messaging and share competitors in targeting.

keyQuestions.question: Does the extended-release program change the competitive picture?
keyQuestions.answer: Potentially, for the prophylaxis market specifically. A less-frequent oral dose would be a meaningful improvement over once-daily Orladeyo and raise the bar for KVD824. Less relevant to sebetralstat on-demand positioning.

name: Pharvaris
oneLineDescription: Clinical-stage company developing oral bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist deucrictibant for both HAE on-demand and prophylaxis.
executiveSummary: Pharvaris is the most direct future competitor to sebetralstat. Deucrictibant is being developed in parallel for HAE on-demand and prophylaxis, with Phase III RAPIDe-3 (on-demand) readout anticipated in 2026. A positive readout and timely filing would bring a second oral on-demand therapy to market within 18 to 24 months of Pharma Inc, with a different mechanism (B2 receptor antagonism vs kallikrein inhibition) that could support head-to-head positioning debates. This is the competitor to track most closely.

keyQuestions.question: What is the realistic deucrictibant on-demand launch timing?
keyQuestions.answer: Assuming a positive RAPIDe-3 readout in Q3 2026 and rolling filing under Fast Track, US launch is plausible H2 2027. EU launch likely Q1 to Q2 2028. This gives Pharma Inc an 18 to 24 month first-mover window in on-demand.

keyQuestions.question: How will mechanism differentiation play out commercially?
keyQuestions.answer: Prescriber response to B2 receptor antagonism vs kallikrein inhibition will be shaped by real-world performance, not pre-launch mechanism debates. Early PRO data and real-world time-to-relief comparisons will matter more than MoA at launch.

keyQuestions.question: What is the biggest risk if RAPIDe-3 reads out stronger than Phase II suggested?
keyQuestions.answer: Deucrictibant being positioned as the 'next-generation oral' relative to sebetralstat. This risk is moderate but real; the mitigation is depth of real-world and PRO evidence for sebetralstat by H2 2027.

keyQuestions.question: Could Pharvaris be acquired before launch?
keyQuestions.answer: Plausible. Large rare-disease players (including Takeda) with commercial infrastructure could be motivated acquirers. An acquisition would change the launch economics and competitive intensity materially.

name: Ionis Pharmaceuticals
oneLineDescription: Donidalorsen (Dawnzera) launched 2025, RNA-based mechanism with differentiated MOA.
executiveSummary: Ionis brought the first antisense oligonucleotide therapy for HAE prophylaxis to market in 2025 with Dawnzera, marketed in partnership with Otsuka. The asset offers monthly subcutaneous dosing and a mechanistically differentiated approach via prekallikrein mRNA knockdown. Early commercial signals point to methodical uptake in centers familiar with antisense therapeutics. Mechanism novelty anchors the commercial narrative; no oral or on-demand HAE programs are signalled. (illustrative)

name: Adverum Biotechnologies
oneLineDescription: Gene therapy approach targeting long-term HAE control with single administration.
executiveSummary: Adverum is developing an AAV-based gene therapy for HAE intended to deliver durable kallikrein pathway modulation from a single administration. The program remains preclinical to early clinical stage, with first-in-human dosing not yet publicly disclosed. Adverum is one of several emerging gene therapy entrants exploring HAE as a target indication; commercial impact, if any, is unlikely before the early 2030s. (illustrative)

name: Intellia Therapeutics
oneLineDescription: NTLA-2002 in Phase 2, CRISPR-based gene editing targeting KLKB1.
executiveSummary: Intellia's NTLA-2002 is the most clinically advanced gene-editing program in HAE, using in vivo CRISPR to knock out the KLKB1 gene encoding prekallikrein. Phase II results have shown sustained attack rate reduction after a single infusion, generating high physician and investor interest. Commercial uptake will depend on long-term safety, infusion logistics, and payer acceptance of upfront cost models. Realistic commercial entry is mid-to-late decade. (illustrative)

name: Astria Therapeutics
oneLineDescription: STAR-0215 in Phase 2, long-acting anti-MASP-2 monoclonal antibody.
executiveSummary: Astria is developing STAR-0215, a long-acting monoclonal antibody intended to enable extended subcutaneous dosing intervals (quarterly or longer) for HAE prophylaxis. Phase II readouts have supported continued development, and Astria has signalled commercial intent through investments in medical affairs and access teams. The program is positioned to compete on dosing convenience against existing biweekly and monthly prophylaxis options. No oral on-demand program is visible. (illustrative)
